abstract: We study coloring extensions over explicit sixteen-vertex cores in the order-twenty Earth–Moon problem. Let $Q_b=F_8(1,b)$, for $b=1,2$, be the exceptional graph formed from two seven-cliques, a complete cross-pair between parts of sizes one and $b$, and a final vertex adjacent to the complementary parts. Put $F_b=K_1\vee Q_b$, a sixteen-vertex graph with seventy edges. Let a $K_9$-free graph $G$ on twenty vertices with at most $108$ edges split into a spanning augmentation of $F_b$, one vertex $z$, and an independent triple $S$ whose vertices have degree at least nine. We prove nine-colorability for $b=1$ whenever $z$ has at least six core neighbors, and for $b=2$ whenever it has at least ten. The first condition follows from minimum degree nine; the second follows from $d_G(z)\ge13$. We absorb $z$ into the colored core and assign nonnegative integer weights to the resulting color partitions, reducing extension to three independent blocking neighborhoods. Conditioning on actual additional core edges resolves failed union bounds. Complete labeled-neighborhood and edge-orbit checks certify 249 neighborhood classes and 966 strict inequalities for $b=1$, and 166 classes and 184 inequalities for $b=2$. Every count in the second result is independently recomputed using direct coloring-support bitsets. Portable verifiers require no optimizer, SAT solver or external graph census. These results exclude one sixteen-core type completely and restrict another high-degree slice; the unrestricted Earth–Moon problem remains open.
